{"channel": "linkedin", "post": "Asking one prompt to write, fact-check, and design content fails every time.

We learned this while turning two-hour operator interviews into articles and carousels.

Our first setup used one giant prompt. It ran fast, but it hallucinated statistics, buried key points, and drifted off brand.

We fixed it by splitting the job across seven small, specialized agents. Here is how to structure that workflow:

1. Separate drafting from verification.
One agent drafts the text. A second agent verifies every single claim against the transcript. A third agent checks editorial tone and rejects any draft that cuts more than half the original material.

2. Match the model to the task.
Orchestration, drafting, and editing require heavy judgment. Run those on higher-tier models like Gemini Pro. High-frequency tasks like scouting and social formatting run faster on lightweight models like Flash.

3. Let code own visual design.
Models struggle with visual consistency. Our social copy agent only returns text inside strict JSON fields. A deterministic renderer places that text onto fixed templates. The AI never touches a hex code or layout setting.

4. Move the human from writer to reviewer.
The agents produce the draft, the image, and the slides. Everything lands in a central review queue. Nothing publishes until an operator checks and approves it.

If an automated workflow is failing, stop adding instructions to one prompt. Break the job into single-task steps instead.

Save this framework for when you build your next content pipeline.", "cta": "Save this framework for when you build your next content pipeline."}
